content: Giardiasis is an intestinal infection caused by Giardia lamblia, a flagellated protozoan parasite. It is a globally prevalent disease, particularly in areas with poor sanitation. The infection can be classified as acute (lasting 2–4 weeks) or chronic (lasting more than 4 weeks) based on the duration of symptoms. Risk factors for developing giardiasis include recent hiking or camping, immunosuppression, young age (especially children under 5 years), exposure to infected individuals, consumption of unsafe water, recent unprotected anal or oral-anal sexual contact, and travel to developing countries. Transmission occurs primarily through the fecal-oral route via contaminated water, food, or direct person-to-person contact. It is also a zoonotic infection, with animals such as beavers, dogs, cats, horses, and cattle serving as reservoirs. After transmission, Giardia colonizes the human intestine and adheres to the epithelial lining using a ventral adhesive disc. The pathogenesis involves increased pro-apoptotic processes, loss of intestinal epithelial barrier integrity, hypersecretion of electrolytes, and heightened exposure of luminal antigens to subepithelial immune cells. This leads to local inflammation, CD8+ T-cell activation, and diffuse shortening of microvilli, impairing nutrient absorption and exacerbating symptoms. Patients may remain asymptomatic for 1–3 weeks post-infection. Early symptoms include acute, watery diarrhea, bloating, and abdominal cramping, which are often self-limiting. If untreated, a subset of patients may develop chronic giardiasis, characterized by persistent diarrhea, anorexia, weight loss, malaise, and failure to thrive. Chronic cases may also involve complications affecting the gallbladder, pancreas, or eyes. The prognosis is generally excellent, but recurrence is common, especially in children, even with optimal treatment. The diagnosis of giardiasis requires the detection of Giardia parasites in at least one of three stool samples collected on separate days. Stool ova and parasite (O&P) examination detects approximately 80% of cases due to intermittent cyst excretion. Fecal immunoassays or molecular testing, such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR), may be used for further confirmation or subtype identification. Blood tests are typically unremarkable. Additional diagnostic studies, such as the string test, D-xylose absorption test, or small bowel biopsy, may be considered in cases with negative stool findings or persistent symptoms despite treatment. Treatment involves antimicrobial therapy, with options including metronidazole, albendazole, or quinacrine. Pediatric patients may also be treated with furazolidone or nitazoxanide. Patients should be monitored for persistent symptoms, which may indicate treatment failure, or for recurrence of symptoms after therapy. There is no vaccine available for giardiasis, and prophylactic measures are not recommended. Preventive strategies focus on hygiene practices, such as regular handwashing and consuming safe drinking water, to reduce the risk of transmission. Historically, the trophozoite form of Giardia was first observed in 1681 by Antonie van Leeuwenhoek in his own diarrheal stool. The organism was initially named Cercomonas intestinalis by Lambl in 1859 and later renamed Giardia lamblia in 1915 in honor of Professor Alfred Giard and Dr. Ferdinand Lambl.
